abstractText:
Plastics that can conduct both electrons and ions are important for numerous applications such as bioelectronic sensors that convert biological nerve impulses into signals readable by digital electronics, energy storage devices that can deliver high currents for short times, and next-generation computers that mimic the function of the brain. One of the factors limiting technological developments in these fields is limited understanding of how ions inject into and transport within these semiconducting plastics. This project addresses this question by analyzing polymers (plastics) at the nanometer scale using advanced microscopy techniques. These methods can determine where polymers are swelling from ion injection and can correlate that response with the chemical signature of the ion using infrared light, also at the nanoscale. The microscopic information is then compared to transistor measurements to gain a fundamental understanding of how the polymer processing and structure influences ion motion. The scientific knowledge from this project enables better design and processing/manufacturing of polymers for the applications noted above. The project additionally builds upon the track record of the principal investigator in education by enabling development of new outreach materials such as polymer electrochemistry kits that are suitable for integration into existing outreach programs and networks. The project also provides direct support for undergraduate research through continuation of the successful partnership with the Rainier Scholars organization to provide pathways to assist under-represented groups and first-generation college students succeed in the sciences. 


The scientific goal of this project is to gain a fundamental understanding of the structure/function relationships controlling ion injection in pi-conjugated polymers operating as mixed ionic/electronic conductors while using blended organic electrochemical transistors as an experimental testbed. These polymers and blends typically exhibit features on the scale of tens of nanometers, and therefore this project uses advanced scanning probe microscopy tools to investigate the ion transport process at the nanoscale. Conjugated polymers have emerged as promising electronic and photonic materials for transducing signals at the interface between the biological and digital environments, and the proposed project will explore fundamental structure/function properties of these materials relevant to these applications in a way that is distinct from other efforts through a combination of unique local and bulk methods. Specifically, the project will: 1) use a new method, photoinduced force microscopy (PiFM), to make nanoscale maps probing how local chemical structure and morphology combine to affect local ion injection; 2) apply electrochemical strain microscopy (ESM) to measure local swelling due to ion uptake in homopolymers, block copolymers, and blends; and, 3) do so while exploring new blend and composite architectures as a means to overcome the bottlenecks of existing materials performance. Notably, this project uses nanoscale infrared microscopy to probe blends of conducting polymers and ionic conductors to test the hypothesis that decoupling the high electronic mobility component and high ionic mobility component can enable improved electrochemical transistors. The principal investigator has shown in previous work that ion injection and electronic mobility are often anti-correlated in mixed conductors, which serves as a device bottleneck. These experiments yield a distinct set of measurements that enable multimodal analysis of the structure-function relationships underpinning ion injection. The project provides important insight into how mobility and volumetric capacitance in mixed ionic-electronic conductors are related, and whether it is possible to rationally improve conducting polymers and polymer blends design by focusing on how ions move into the polymer from the ground up.

projectOutComesReport:
Plastics that can conduct both electrons and ions are important for numerous applications including bioelectronic sensors that convert biological nerve impulses into signals that are readable by digital electronics, energy storage devices that can deliver high currents for short times, and next-generation computers that mimic the function of the brain. These materials offer much technological promise; however, one of the factors limiting technological developments in these fields is our limited understanding of how ions inject into and transport within these semiconducting plastic materials.

In this project, supported by a grant from the Division of Materials Research, we have investigated the fundamental properties that control ion transport in soft polymeric semiconducting materials. We studied these materials using a combination of microscopy and measurement methods like optical microscopy, atomic force microscopy, and device data. Using these techniques, we studied several different materials, revealing new insights the properties that control the ion injection process, as well as the ion expulsion process. First, we combined optical measurements with atomic force microscopy (AFM) techniques to probe the effects of using polymer nanowire films on the kinetics of ion injection. Polymers normally form an amorphous film but can be engineered to form long wire-like strands. We showed that ions more easily penetrate the nanowire matrix compared to an amorphous film, causing a significant improvement in the speed of turn on due to faster ion injection, and we used combined AFM with infrared laser excitation to directly show that ions aggregate on the surface in the non-nanowire film. Next, we worked with a range of different polymers to understand the effect of changing the chemistry of the sidechain on the speed of switching. By changing the position of an oxygen atom on the sidechain of a semiconducting polymer called polythiophene, we could observe significant changes in ion injection speed and transistor performance. Next, we applied these techniques to a polymer that does not have any sidechains yet is an efficient ion transport material, a fact that has confused researchers for many years. We showed that this sidechain-free polymer, called BBL, can swell in salt solution as soon as a voltage is applied to the water, allowing for ions to penetrate between crystallites due to this swelling effect. This observation provided key insight into how to design polymers without sidechains that still work with ions. Lastly, we recently completed work studying the asymmetric kinetics of ion injection into conducting polymers. Researchers have commonly observed this phenomenon, where ions are very slow to enter a material but quick to leave the material (“doping” and “dedoping,” respectively). We used optical microscopy on devices to show the ion injection profiles in realtime, and we used these data to develop a model that explains why ions inject into the film relatively slowly.

Our reports provide a set of work that help explain the different properties that control ion injection, from exploring the polymer structure and sidechain chemistry to fundamental studies of the ion injection/expulsion process. These experiments combined AFM measurements and optical studies, and the work generated by this grant has laid the groundwork for future studies into understanding how to exploit kinetics for devices that mimic memory cells.

In addition, this project supported workforce development through the interdisciplinary training of several graduate and undergraduate students, and supported the core Ph.D. work of 2 students who graduated with their doctorates (one is now working in the U.S. semiconductor industry, and one now working for a U.S. national laboratory),  one student who graduated with a masters degree, and multiple summer undergraduates students who were recruited through partnerships with local organizations that focus on provide opportunities to hard-working, low-income students, many of whom are the first in their families to attend college.

abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is the development of technology for smart street parking. An estimated thirty percent of all traffic in the average U.S. city consists of vehicles searching for parking spots. Finding street parking in big cities can be challenging; the time spent searching is long, signage may be confusing or misinterpreted, and errors can be expensive (ticketed or towed). This could be mitigated with: (i) Street parking planning identifying suitable parking areas in advance of a trip, and (ii) curb-surfing verify the parking rules. The estimated market size for smart parking is $3.8 B.  The proposed technology offers these two essential street parking services to drivers, delivery providers, and smart vehicle/smart city infrastructure through apps and APIs.

This I-Corps project is based on the development of a series of machine learning algorithms and IoT technologies. Specifically, the novel techniques are developed and used in the following steps:  (i) Street parking sign detection from pictures/videos taken by cameras on smartphones/vehicles; (ii) text recognition from the detected street parking signs; (iii) Natural language processing (NLP) used to generate parking rules; (iv) allowed parking time calculation; and (v) trust evaluation in crowdsourcing. This technology focuses on street parking sign recognition and interpretation. Although there are many AI-based object detection and text recognition techniques, typically they do not work well in these applications as the text on street parking signs is different and signs vary among cities. In addition, the technology addresses the challenge of distinguishing parking signs from other co-located signs.

projectOutComesReport:
The team built a solution for smart street parking.The goal of this I-Corps Teams project is to develop a feasible plan to commercialize the technology and develop a team to be capable of executing the plan. 

Intellectual Merits:

The team built a series of systems for smart street parking via jointly utilizing machine learning and IoT technologies. Specifically, the solution includes: a street parking inventory database for cities, a website of street parking inventory management for cities, a website of street parking planning for drivres, and a mobile App for street parking navigation. The key novel techniques for building the solution are the four pipelined algorithms:  (i) the street parking sign detection algorithm; (ii) the street parking sign text recognition algorithm,  (iii) the  street parking rule generation algorithm, and  (iv) the real-time allowed parking time calculation algorithm. Our solution is the first one that can accurately find the street parking signs, read the street parking signs, and generate the street parking rules from the videos taken by an off-the-shelf dash cam.

Broader Impacts:

Finding street parking in big cities is challenging. Moreover, street parking can be expensive (ticketed/towed) due to how easily drivers can misunderstand of the street parking signs that can be very complex to read and understand. The solution provided by the team can help drivers know where the street parking spots, which will fit their parking needs, are and navigate them to the spots. Drivers' time and gas can be significantly saved. The soultion can also help cities reduce the traffic, greenhouse gas emission, and illegal parking. This project is undertaken by a team including female entrepreneurs and minorities. The students were trained for AI and system technology development and bussiness development. The team has secured a paid pilot project with a city for buidling a street parking inventory management system.

abstractText:
Much remains to be learned about communicating science effectively. When people process complex information, they often simplify it in order to understand it. To facilitate this process, simplification is necessary in almost all science communication. However, the exact form of simplification is key, especially with controversial issues.. This is because some simplifications may confuse people, or even be exploited to intentionally mislead them. This project tests risk communication strategies designed to address the cognitive simplifications that underlie factually erroneous beliefs about scientific issues in situations where such misunderstandings may be likely to lead to suboptimal intentions and decisions. The research also tests the effects of explicitly acknowledging scientific uncertainty on trust in the information provided. Previous research shows that overstating the certainty of the science may invite skepticism.  In sum, this project will contribute to a better understanding of how lay audiences think about complex scientific issues and uncertainty as well as to the development of risk communication strategies based on those principles. The project will identify strategies that can be adopted by science educators and risk communicators to help audiences to understand complex risks that subsume critical science elements. 

Successful science and risk communication depend critically on first understanding how people process complex information. When people think about complex scientific issues, they tend to use shortcuts and more readily accept information consistent with their own prior beliefs.  Communication strategies that are guided by cognitive principles can minimize the weaknesses and capitalize on the strengths of the human information processing system. This project will develop and test communication strategies targeting known simplifications that tend to reduce processing load, but also can lead to misunderstandings that reduce the perceived seriousness and urgency of the risk. Because people may not be aware of the assumptions upon which their understanding is based, providing explanations illuminating those steps may allow non-experts to achieve an unbiased and better-rounded understanding of the issue. As a result, they may come to better appreciate the scientifically-assessed seriousness of the problem and to better identify effective mitigative actions.  These hypotheses will be tested on nationally representative samples, in experiments that systematically examine the extent to which targeted communication strategies influence trust, individual reasoning, mental models, attitudes, emotions, and decisions, controlling for key factors previously identified as being associated with science-oriented attitudes, including political ideology, age, race and ethnicity. The cognitive experimental approach proposed here is novel and will make important contributions to the psychology of risk communication, as well as to the study of higher order cognition (e.g., decision making) by applying interventions based on dual process theories and mental model constructs.

projectOutComesReport:
Although simplification is inherent in how people process complex information and therefore necessary in almost all science communication, the exact form of simplification is key, especially with controversial issues like climate change. This is because some simplifications may confuse people, or worse, may be exploited to mislead them, and thereby reduce the perceived seriousness of the risk. Three such widely held misunderstandings are that: (1) decreasing emissions means a concurrent decrease in greenhouse gas concentrations, allowing for a wait-and-see attitude; (2) current global warming is due to "natural" climate variability, reducing human responsibility; and (3) greenhouse gases are equivalent to common air pollution (i.e., smog, particulate matter) implying similar rapid resolution. This project tested communications strategies designed to address the cognitive simplifications that underlie these beliefs.  

The major goals of this project were to (1) test candidate risk communication strategies designed to address specific cognitive simplifications that might affect understanding of the scientific issue of climate change, to learn (2) whether risk communications addressing these cognitive simplifications can correct erroneous beliefs about scientific issues such as climate change, (3) whether correcting such beliefs affects attitudes toward the information, the scientific issue, or policies to mitigate risks stemming from the issue, and (4) whether explicitly acknowledging scientific uncertainty in this context increases trust in the information provided.

We conducted three national experiments to test these ideas, two with U.S. national online convenience samples and the third with a U.S. nationally representative sample. In these experiments we tested the following general hypotheses:  Simple but accurate scientific explanations, targeting the three misunderstandings described above by pointing out each step in the reasoning process, would help participants to better appreciate the mechanisms and or effects of climate change, and would also change participants willingness to support climate friendly policies and decisions.  We also hypothesized that acknowledging uncertainty would increase trust in the information provided.

We developed the explanations in consultations with climate scientists. In initial testing the Delay and Pollution explanations appeared to be effective, the visual explanation we had developed to address the natural variability explanation less so. The Delay explanation entailed describing the long delay between carbon emission reduction and global temperature decline, by pointing out that “If we start reducing CO2 emissions today, and reduce them every year, concentrations in the atmosphere would continue to rise for 100 years; the global average temperature would rise for 200 years, and only fall after 300 years.” The Pollution explanation compared conventional air pollution and greenhouse gasses on each of typical types of concepts found in mental models of hazardous processes, such as where they come from (sources), where they go (sinks), how they can or cannot be detected, how they behave in the atmosphere, and what effects they have on the environment and humans, highlighting similarities and differences between the two.

As predicted, the Delay and Pollution explanations effectively reduced the delay and air pollution misconceptions and improved understanding of climate change.  Few participants were familiar with the long delay between reduction in carbon emissions and reduction in global warming prior to reading the explanation. After reading the Delay explanation, a large majority understood this.  The Pollution explanation also improved accuracy, especially among liberals and moderates who were more inclined to conflate climate change and air pollution pre-experimentally. Adding explicit acknowledgement of uncertainty to the explanations had no discernible effect.

Furthermore, agreement with policy strategies such as  “fund research to make renewable energy technologies cheaper and more effective” and “enforce all current air pollution control standards” was higher among those who had read the Delay explanation than for those who read only baseline information, or no information.  In addition, both those who read the Delay explanation and those who read the Pollution explanation rated higher agreement with “Fund research and development of new technologies to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere,” than those who received no information or only baseline information. 

The public deserves access to valid, understandable scientific information on critical issues that impact their well-being. Indeed, a common goal of science communication is to inform individual and policy decisions for consequential problems such as climate change. Although attitudes toward climate change have been studied extensively, very little research has focused on the cognitive mechanisms and conceptual structures that support understanding of climate issues or on communication strategies that are targeted to address them. This project focused on these. Although people may differ in terms of their attitudes, they are similar in how they process information in domains in which they are not experts. In two national survey experiments, targeted explanations designed to address common but potentially misleading cognitive simplifications improved understanding of climate change.

abstractText:
This project investigates instances of convergent or translational research within and across the natural, engineering and social sciences.  Scientific research increasingly relies on collaboration across many different areas of expertise. When there is a need to do research that translates expertise, tools, and analytic techniques across research areas or projects, it must be convergent and presents challenges for scientists who are trying to collaborate in new ways. This project aims to investigate new dynamics of collaboration emerging around processes and goals for convergent research, which has become a central plank of recent NSF efforts. This research will inform science policy and regulatory environments to help develop sustainable and productive research organizations, platforms, infrastructure, and convergent tools.

The focus of this research is on exemplary experts who conduct translational research, their practices, organizational forms, technical tools and architectures. It will study experts in ocean science, radio astronomy, and data science among others. The goal is to understand and analyze practices of convergence, recurrent challenges, and technological architectures, in order to support and enhance activities that advance science. The methods used are comparative, archival and ethnographic. The ethnographic work is both multi-sited (operating across multiple research locales) and multi-scalar (exploring phenomena nested at multiple scales).  Both elements are crucial to the comparative analysis of convergence activities.  At a higher and more general level, the research  explores network-based dynamics and convergence actors operating within and across the sites of investigation.  At a lower and more specific level, it drills down to consider in greater detail the local convergence adopted in select network micro-sites.  Findings will contribute to the sociotechnical design of tools and infrastructure, the human-computer interaction field of computer supported cooperative work and science and technology studies.

abstractText:
The outbreak of novel coronavirus disease (COVID-19) has caused a global pandemic. Knowledge on the molecular basis of novel coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2) related protein complexes is essential to providing insight of the virus and how it infects human cells, a first step in developing novel drugs and vaccines to combat SARS-CoV-2. This study will enable development of all-atom structure prediction of CoV-related protein complexes, including complex surfaces of human cells the virus infects. Prediction results will be broadly and quickly disseminated through interactive web applications to maximize the impact of the research. The results will lead to a broad range of biomedical applications, such as a better understanding of important biological functions, disease processes, development of novel drugs and vaccines, and improved preventive therapies leading to reduced health care costs. 

The project seeks to study ab initio all-atom structure prediction of CoV-related protein complexes based on electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM). Methods based on the state-of-the-art technologies of image processing for pre-processing the data, deep learning for complex structure prediction, and dynamic optimization for final refinement to reveal fundamental mechanisms of CoV-related macromolecules will be developed. The project will also provide an open-source and interactive web portal for public access of the developed tools. The work could have immediate impact on steps taken to halt the spread of SARS-CoV-2 and the current pandemic. Training opportunities for students at all levels, particularly women and underrepresented minorities will also be carried out. The results of the project can be found at: http://faculty.washington.edu/dongsi.

This RAPID award is made by the Infrastructure Innovation for Biological Research (IIBR Informatics) Program in the Division of Biological Infrastructure, using funds from the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act.

projectOutComesReport:
Intellectual merit:

This project developed methods of geometric modeling, artificial intelligence, and computational biology to provide a biophysical characterization of SARS-CoV-2 and other CoV-related protein complexes using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) (Figure 1). This project revealed information that is relevant to the function and potential targeting and disruption of the viruses.

We developed fast, accurate, and fully automated de novo protein large complex structure prediction from a 3D electron density map and conducted case studies on CoV-related data (Pfab et al. PNAS 2021). We introduced deep learning methods and optimization techniques to predict the locations of atoms, secondary structure elements, and amino acid types. The work has been highlighted in Nature Computational Science (Chirigati, F. Predicting protein structure from cryo-EM data. Nat Comput Sci 1, 96, 2021).

We developed an interactive web portal https://deeptracer.uw.edu/covid for public access to the CoV-related predictions. The work could have an immediate impact on steps taken to halt the spread of SARS-CoV-2 and the current pandemic. The web portal automatically updates the predictions for the new CoV-related EM data. The interactive web applications provide workflows for stages from data uploading, modeling, and tools that facilitate visualization and evaluation of the prediction process. The predictions include atomic protein structures of SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, H-CoV, MHV, AIBV, FIPV, PD-CoV, PEDV, Spike, Non-Spike, ACE2 receptor, Fab, Polymerase, Ribosome. Which are the key entities involved in the molecular mechanism of COVID-19. Our work successfully built the atomic models for the CoV-related EM maps, especially for the ones that have no previous deposited model structure available in the data bank.

 

Broader of impacts:

We remain steadfast and dedicated to the global fight against SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) with our DeepTracer web server and COV-related prediction web portal. The project and results could have led to a broad range of biomedical applications, such as a better understanding of important biological functions, disease processes, the development of novel drugs and vaccines, and improved preventive therapies leading to reduced health care costs. The methods and results developed in this project have been broadly disseminated to multiple communities including biology, biochemistry, health science, and pharmaceutical sciences. The data mining and artificial intelligence techniques developed in this project are very likely to be applicable for solving the computational problems from the closely related 3D volume data generated from different imaging techniques, and those in which one has to deal with data errors and noises.

The research has concretely demonstrated the applicability of data mining from the 3DEMDaraResource and the use of sophisticated deep learning methods for fast, accurate, and fully automated protein structure determination from COVID-related EM data. The computational methods and tools developed in this project have been used to interpret large molecular assemblies that have important biological functions such as viruses and cellular machines. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for designing drugs and vaccines for current and future pandemics.

The project has been supporting the mentorship and training of high school, undergraduate, and graduate students both in the conduct of research and in the mentorship of more junior students. This project attracted more than thirty students in multiple disciplines including Computer Science, Biology, Chemistry, Physics, Health Science, Information Science, and Math. Students have been involved in the project in the frontend and backend design, research and product development, testing, and publishing. This project also involved female students and students from underrepresented ethnic groups. The PI engaged in local, national, and global community outreach activities to disseminate the broad impact of this project and the value of NSF.

abstractText:
Human contacts underlie the spread of any infectious diseases including COVID-19. For COVID-19, the widely implemented social distancing policies are designed precisely to drastically reduce individual travels and the resulting contacts. In a number of States, these policies have effectively reduced the peak number of infections. These policies have also come with huge costs on the society, economy and people’s lives: US economy has largely come to a halt and the number of unemployment claims has now exceeded the worst of the 2008-2009 financial crisis. This rapid COVID-19 application will develop a novel meta-population level model simulating the spread of COVID-19 and utilize reinforcement learning to explore optimal congregation restriction policies for social distancing. 

The technical approach will develop an SIQR (Susceptible, Infected, Quarantined, and Recovered) model integrated with reinforcement learning for continuous monitoring and policy adjustment. The SIQR model is built on the classic literature of the SIR (susceptible, infectious and recovered) and SEIR (susceptible, exposed, infectious, and recovered) models and enhances their capability to capture the unique quarantine features for COVID-19. The key focus of the proposed project is on the connection of the SIQR model to reinforcement learning to realize a control loop that provides optimal policy in spite of sparse and noisy observations. This is an important contribution to this emerging, interdisciplinary science of infectious disease modeling and control. The results of this project will have both immediate importance for designing the response to COVID-19 and also contribute to the broader development of an interdisciplinary education and research program involving infectious disease modeling, reinforcement learning and machine learning of big data.

projectOutComesReport:
Background: 

Since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, social distancing has been key to curb the spread of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). Social distancing policies around the world have largely been made based upon reported case data: the rise/fall of cases are coupled with recommendations for tighter/looser policies. It is widely known that underreporting exists in case data, due to limited test capacity, asymptotic cases or unwillingness to test etc. Yet, there is little to no understanding of how underreporting in case data may affect the performance of social distancing policies designed using such data.

 

Objective:

This study aims to evaluate the impacts of underreporting on social distancing policies that are designed based on various rationales and the resulting disease trajectories. If the policy maker is aware of the underreporting issue, efforts could be made to correct it. Whether correction of underreporting mitigates its impacts is also investigated.

 

Methods:

The project developed an SIQR (Susceptible, Infected, Quarantined, and Recovered) model integrated with three controllers for continuous monitoring and policy adjustment. The SIQR model is built on the classic literature of the SIR (susceptible, infectious and recovered) and SEIR (susceptible, exposed, infectious, and recovered) models and enhances their capability to capture the unique ?quarantine? features for COVID-19. The project designs a setting with 100,000 population and starting case numbers, and selects three policy-making rationales (called ?controllers?) from existing literature: an Flattening-the-Curve (FC) controller that maximizes allowable transmission rate while ensuring hospital capacity is not exceeded; a Time-Limited-Intervention (TLI) controller to minimize the number of infectious people with policies of fixed durations; and a Minimizing-Health-and-Economic-Costs-with-Reinforcement-Learning (MC-RL) controller to minimize weighted public health and economic costs. For each controller, the recommended social distancing policies and consequent disease trajectories are compared among different scenarios where there is no underreporting, where there is underreporting but without correcting it, and where there is underreporting with corrections.

 

Results:

Under the influence of underreporting, the FC controller is found to recommend stricter policies; the TLI controller recommends stricter policies at the beginning but more relaxed policies later; and the MC-RL controller recommends stricter policies when hospital capacity is low and more relaxed policies otherwise. For disease trajectories, the FC and TLI controllers result in higher and later peaks under the influence of underreporting; and the MC-RL controller will result in more people being infectious if policies are designed with underreported data, especially when hospital capacity is low. Correction of underreporting mitigates the above impacts of underreporting for the FC and TLI controllers, but for the MC-RL controller, whether correction mitigates or exaggerates those impacts varies with the controller?s parameters that define the hospital capacity in a region and severity of the disease.

Conclusions:

Policies designed using underreported data cannot achieve preset control objectives, and how the disease trajectory will unfold under such policies may bring unexpected outcomes and catch policy makers off guard. Our findings emphasize the high stakes if the underreporting issue is ignored or under-/over-corrected in the response to resurgence of COVID-19 or possible outbreaks of new infectious diseases.

abstractText:
The mechanisms that underlie the ability to acquire new knowledge about the external world, to remember it, and to use the information to behave appropriately and adaptively is a long-standing interest of humankind. Experience-dependent plasticity of the synaptic connections between neurons is generally accepted as the cellular mechanism with which a neural circuitry acquires and stores new information, commonly known as learning and memory. This project studies the homeostatic mechanisms that regulate the positive feedback nature of synaptic plasticity, that is, the mechanisms that bound activity levels within an appropriate dynamic range to preserve the ability of plasticity near saturation of activity as well as near absence of activity. How such complex homeostatic tasks are accomplished in the brain is poorly understood. Here, these homeostatic mechanisms are studied in the cerebellum of the mormyrid fish, whose cerebellar circuitry as well as its outputs and inputs are well defined and accessible for detailed examination. Using a combination of electrophysiological, imaging, and pharmacological approaches, the investigators characterize changes in the input/output relationships of cerebellar Purkinje cells during long-term potentiation and long-term depression of synaptic input to these cells, and begin to elucidate the underlying mechanisms. The results will have broad implications for understanding of the neural substrates of learning and memory.  The project also involves outreach to Seattle area elementary and middle schools, to teach about behavioral plasticity of electric fish.
 
Synaptic plasticity is generally accepted as the cellular mechanism with which a neural circuitry acquires and stores new information, commonly known as learning and memory. The most studied forms of plasticity include Hebbian long-term potentiation (LTP) and depression (LTD). Hebbian plasticity operates in a positive loop, leading to runaway neuronal activity and requiring additional compensatory processes to stabilize the neural circuitry. Many forms of homeostatic plasticity have been suggested as providing such compensatory role. However, unlike Hebbian synaptic plasticity, the demonstrated forms of homeostatic plasticity require very different time courses to be induced (hours to days versus seconds to minutes). Furthermore, modeling studies suggest that the slow evolution of homeostatic plasticity observed in experiments is insufficient to prevent instabilities of Hebbian plasticity. This project examines rapid, compensatory synaptic processes that could potentially prevent the instabilities associated with the positive feedback nature of Hebbian plasticity. Using dual whole-cell recording in slice reparations of the mormyrid cerebellum, the investigator has found that the strength of a Purkinje cells output synapses onto their target cells is up- and downregulated following LTD and LTP at the same cell’s input synapses, respectively. Here, a combination of in-vitro electrophysiological, imaging, and pharmacological approaches extend these observations to examine the characteristics and mechanisms underlying this bidirectional regulation of a cell’s output transmission following Hebbian plasticity at its input synapses. Establishment of this form of rapid, dynamic homeostatic plasticity and its underlying mechanisms will yield valuable insights into elementary processes of synaptic plasticity.

jrnl.auth: Magnus, Gerhard and Xing, Junling and Zhang, Yueping and Han, Victor Z.

program: NEURAL SYSTEMS, UNDERGRADUATE EDUCATION
projectOutComesReport:
Synaptic plasticity is generally believed to be one of the cellular mechanisms underlying learning and memory in the brain. Its distribution and molecular mechanisms have been well investigated. However, the vast majority, if not all, of such studies, have focused on synapses,  while learning and memory are characterized in terms of neural circuitry or at network levels in general. Thus, the question remains as to how a subcellular change such as synaptic plasticity is incorporated into a specific neural circuitry leading to learning and memory.

The present study utilizes dual-cell recording from a slice preparation of the mormyrid cerebellum. In the cerebellum of this fish, efferent cells migrate into the Purkinje cell layer during development instead of forming deep cerebellar nuclei, as in mammals. This more compact cerebellar circuitry allows us to simultaneously record from not only PC-PC pairs, but also from PCs and their specific efferent cell targets, which is not possible in mammalian cerebellar preparations. Thus, synaptic plasticity such as long-term depression (LTD) or potentiation (LTP) can be induced at the PF synapses of a Purkinje cell, while the output of the same Purkinje cell on a target cell be recorded simultaneously. We can thereby monitor the dynamic changes at a Purkinje cell’s input synapses and the effects of the same cell’s output onto a specific target at the same time.

Our unexpected results indicate that PF-LTD of a Purkinje cell typically accompanies the potentiation of same Purkinje cell’s output onto its target cell, while PF-LTP accompanies that output’s depression. To the best of our knowledge, such homeostatic feedback from a cell’s output synapses onto the same cell’s input synapses has not been reported in any other cell types or related structures. In conclusion, we show that  the functional circuitry of a Purkinje cell and its targets may be able stabilize by itself, rather than than being destabilzed or silenced by a “runaway plasticity” of positive and negative feedback loops at PF-PC synapses, as suggested by the Hebbian hypothesis more than half a century ago.

The impact of this project is significant because for the first time it provides experimental evidence that a functional neuronal circuitry can be stabilized by a homeostatic mechanism simultaneously with the induction of synaptic plasticity.

 

Due to pandemic-related difficulties in obtaining mormyrid fish for our work, we investigated the local circuitry of the adult zebrafish cerebellum as an alternative model system. Our results demonstrated that the Purkinje cells of the adult zebrafish can be morphologically and physiologically classified into 3 or 4 subtypes, suggesting that these subtypes have different input pathways. This is the only species in which a local cerebellar circuitry has been so characterized.

abstractText:
On March 11, 2020 the coronavirus officially became a global pandemic. In the United States the suggestion to practice “social distancing” was replaced by official “stay at home” orders from at least 30 states, and numerous counties and cities. Despite these official orders, people continued to gather in outdoor spaces and in private. Why do they do so? Are they “risk seeking” in the sense that they understand the risk but have decided to take it anyway? Or do they misunderstand the risk of contracting the disease, becoming seriously ill, or spreading it to others? Given the complexity and variability of the information about coronavirus available to the public, misunderstandings are likely. It may be difficult for individuals to assess their own risk of contracting and/or dying from the disease, and particularly difficult to understand the risk of passing it on to others. Nonetheless, one thing is clear: older people are at a greater risk for fatality. The risk for contracting the disease, however, appears to be more evenly distributed across age groups. It is possible that people use an unconscious simplifying strategy focusing on the more dramatic and widely publicized death rates and assume that if they are younger, all risks, including those that they pose to others, are less. The first goal of this project is to assess the perceived risks associated with coronavirus across age groups and determine how risk perception impacts the decisions people make. The second goal is to design and test risk expressions that are understandable to members of the public. Thus, this project makes significant contributions to our understanding of how people make risky decisions in context, based on complex risk information, as well as to the development of communication strategies tailored for different users.
 
Successful risk communication strategies depend upon first understanding how people process complex risk information. In the context of the coronavirus, decision makers must take into account both the risk to themselves as well as the risk to others they may infect if they contract the coronavirus. There are numerous cognitive issues associated with this process that at present are not well understood. In particular, how do people understand related but differing risk estimates? How do they use that information to make precautionary decisions that impact themselves as well as others? This project conducts a series of online studies to determine how people perceive coronavirus risks, separately and in combination, as well as how risk perception impacts their precautionary decisions. Perhaps more importantly, based on preliminary surveys, understandable risk communication expressions are developed and tested experimentally to establish causal links between information expression and risk perception, trust, and decisions. Finally, using a few relevant individual difference measures, the researchers determine whether specific abilities are necessary to process complex numeric risk expressions and whether simplified expressions are better in some cases. The results of this work provide invaluable advice with the potential to save lives. This research can inform best practices in risk communication that have important implications for communicating risks in future outbreaks. Understanding how best to communicate risks to the public and whether communication should be tailored to specific subgroups is critical to avoiding future pandemics.

projectOutComesReport:
Critical to limiting the spread of Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID- 19) and future pandemics is compliance with behavioral recommendations such as mask wearing, vaccination, and social distancing. Compliance may depend upon understanding the seriousness of the health consequences, the likelihood they will occur, and the safety of the measures such as vaccination. We explored these issues in five experiments, the first three focused on risk perception early in the pandemic. The last two investigated messaging to increase vaccination rates.

The statistics that speak to risk in an ongoing pandemic are complex and may be misunderstood. One major goal of the first three studies was to determine how risk messaging, based on the statistics available early in the pandemic, impacted peoples' perception of the likelihood of contracting or dying from COVID-19 and participants' willingness to engage in protective actions like mask wearing and social distancing.

In two online experiments conducted in May and June 2020 with 3,634 Americans, we tested the impact of risk messages on risk perception, willingness to take protective measures (e.g., mask wearing, social distancing), and agreement with government response. The biggest issue at the time was the contrast between the disease outcomes for older and younger people. Therefore, infection messages described the percentage of those older and younger than 50 years of age, among all those who had tested positive for COVID-19. Mortality messages described the percentage of all those who died of COVID-19, who were older and younger than 50. We also tested messages that described both (mortality and infection). We tested numeric expressions that described the percentage in each age group and gist messages that indicated which group was smaller (mortality) or that they were roughly equivalent (infection).

We found for younger participants, providing both mortality and infection statistics in the gist message increased willingness to wear masks indoors, perhaps because it made clear that although they were less likely to die from COVID-19, they were equally likely to be infected and spread it. We also found that government restrictions (social distance, stay at home) were effective. They increased willingness to wear a mask among younger participants and decreased willingness to engage in risk seeking activities (e.g., go to gym) for the group as a whole. Surprisingly, there was no difference detected in effectiveness of restrictions due to political ideology, suggesting that these kinds of measures may be widely, if not universally effective. Although we expected younger participants to be much more willing to engage in risky behaviors than older participants, this was not so. Instead, the largest difference was due to political ideology. Conservatives were much less will willing to engage in protective behaviors like mask wearing than were liberals, although they perceived similar COVID-19 risks.

Two later experiments focused on vaccine-hesitancy among 5,354 unvaccinated Americans in April and July 2021, after those 18 years and older became eligible for the COVID-19 vaccines. Previous research suggested that the greatest barrier to vaccination for some people may be fear of the vaccine itself. This could be due to misunderstandings about the vaccines, arising from complexities of the science involved. Therefore, the goal of these experiments was to test simple explanations correcting known misunderstandings to see if they increased willingness to get the COVID-19 vaccine compared to a no-information group.

Indeed, these unvaccinated individuals were less concerned about the threat of the disease than about the safety of the vaccine. This asymmetry in concerns may be characteristic of the vaccine hesitant and as such, could inform communications strategies going forward. Importantly, in both studies we found that explanations of issues such as the incidence and nature of vaccine side effects and the mechanism by which mRNA vaccines provide protection, presented in everyday language, were effective. They increased willingness to get vaccinated, regardless of political ideology (Figure 1). Interestingly, among the explanations that was most effective was a lengthy text that combined these side effects and mechanism explanations and included refutational text. Refutational text explicitly points out the misunderstanding (Some people think X, but that is not true) and corrects it. Refutational text may be especially effective in cases in which such misunderstandings are repeatedly reinforced and/or based on assumptions of which decision makers are not fully aware. Guiding people through the reasoning process step-by-step may be necessary to correct the misunderstanding and change attitudes.

This research has important implications for communicating information to unvaccinated individuals and communicating health information in general. Although there are many who believe that 'less is more' in risk communication, the research reported here suggests the opposite, that complex scientific explanations can be effective in reducing concerns and increasing willingness to get vaccinated. Such explanations can allow people to appreciate the relevant scientific facts, overcome dangerous misunderstandings, and make better decisions for themselves and others.

abstractText:
Topology is a field of mathematics that studies those properties of a space that remain invariant under stretching or bending. A surface of a fixed topological shape can have many different geometries. For example, a two-dimensional shape with no holes is a topological sphere, which could be a round sphere (like the surface of a planet), a polyhedron (a crystal like-shape with facets), or an ellipsoid (an egg-type shape). A shape with one hole (a torus) could look like an inner tube, a tire, or a hula hoop. The collection of all possible geometries is known as a moduli space, and these spaces occur over and over again in fundamental physical questions. This NSF award provides funding for a project to study questions of what typical, or random, surfaces look like, from the point of view of understanding families of curves on these surfaces. The research and outreach activities are mutually reinforcing; the project highlights bridges between different areas of mathematics, and deep connections between research, mentoring, and public engagement programs in mathematics. In addition the project provide research training opportunities for graduate students.
 
Starting with simple to state problems about counting special trajectories on surfaces whose geometry comes from Euclidean polygons and polyhedra, and motivated by theoretical physics (Newtonian mechanics, electron transport, and supersymmetric quantum field theory), this project connects to fundamental questions in many different areas of mathematics, including Teichmuller and homogeneous dynamics; Diophantine approximation and the geometry of numbers; probabilistic models and limit theorems; and the geometry of moduli spaces of meromorphic differentials on surfaces. Building on his prior collaborative work, the PI plans to explore questions on the counting and distributions of curves in varying geometries on higher-genus surfaces and higher-dimensional tori.

projectOutComesReport:
This project explored counting problems and statistics associated to curves on surfaces, motivated by problems in geometry and dynamical systems. In particular, many of the problems were motivated by simple Newtonian mechanical problems (billiards in polygons) which lead to surprisingly complex mathematics, touching on many different subfields, including geometry, algebraic geometry, dynamical systems, number theory, and others.

My work centers a probabilistic perspective and uses ideas of renormalization to study problems of counting and correlations for curves and special trajectories on surfaces arising from special billiard trajectories, for example. In the attached images, one sees figures from two papers which were written with the support of the grant, one studying trajectories of triply periodic polyhedral surfaces (which arise in the study of electricity and magnetism) and the other associated to studying the movement of particles on the dodecahedron.

In addition to several peer-reviewed papers, this project resulted in a new book (joint with Howard Masur) on Translation Surfaces (which will make the field accessible to a new generation of students), and the research informed several art projects and public-facing works (online videos, exhibits, documentaries, and general interest articles).

The project also enabled the mentorship of several students and postdocs, as well as many undergraduates who worked on experimental and exploratory projects in the mathematical sciences.

Finally, the results of the project have opened up several new vistas in research on the geometry and statistics of curves on surfaces, which we are actively pursuing.

abstractText:
The ability to predict weather across the globe, and sea ice conditions critical for defense and maritime operations in the Arctic, requires observations of surface meteorology and ice/ocean currents. The US Interagency Arctic Buoy Program (USIABP) and International Arctic Buoy Programme (IABP) maintain this fundamental Arctic Observing Network across the expanse of the Arctic Ocean. Observations and data sets produced by Polar Science Center (PSC) and University of Washington Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) for the IABP have led to advancing scientific understanding of regional and global impacts influenced by changes in the Arctic Ocean. Through diverse outreach efforts, the PIs will disseminate their scientific findings in media interviews and participate in the annual Polar Science Weekend and Climate Curiosity Days at Seattle's Pacific Science Center. This project also provides opportunities to Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) based programs that work with high school students to learn about, design and launch buoys, and support US Naval Academy student buoy engineering projects. The researchers have developed a low-cost open source Arctic buoy to gather more data, and are involved in producing a range of data visualization art projects to engage the public with the Arctic through exhibition venues in Canada, Norway, and the US including at the National Academy of Sciences in Washington D.C.

The USIABP will deploy buoys in the increasing areas of open water in the Arctic during summer and has established a semi-permanent test site in Utqiagvik, Alaska, to assess the quality of the instruments now used by the IABP to observe the Arctic Ocean. This project intends to maintain a network of buoys with a spacing of less than 250 km, or more than 200 buoys spread across the Arctic Ocean, and with deployment logistics that include: 1) aircraft landing on the sea ice in the spring; 2) icebreakers deploying buoys for the IABP as opportunities arise; and 3) aircraft dropping buoys onto the sea ice. These observations are assimilated into Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models that are used to forecast weather on synoptic time scales, and into the many long-term atmospheric reanalyses that are used for climate studies. Overall, the observations from the IABP are essential for: 1) monitoring Arctic and global climate change; 2) forcing, assimilation, and validation of global weather and climate models; and 3) validation of satellite derived estimates of sea ice motion, surface temperature, and sea ice thickness. Further, IABP Observations are shared through the IABP server, the World Meteorological Organization and Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission (WMO/IOC) Global Telecommunications System (GTS), and stored in publicly accessible archives including the NSF Arctic Data Center. These observations provide the longest continuing record for the Arctic and have been one of the cornerstones of the Arctic Observing Network for environmental forecasting and studies of climate and climate change.

abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is the development of a biofeedback training tool to increase student academic performance. As pressures to improve academic performance continue to increase, students are increasingly coming to school emotionally unprepared to learn. This is frequently compounded by the lack of a healthy social and emotional environment within the school to support, motivate, and emotionally engage students. As research has illuminated the important connections between emotions, learning, and performance, it has become apparent that effective school-based interventions are needed to foster and integrate students’ emotional, social, and academic development to provide them with tools and skills needed to increase self-awareness and emotional self-management; promote effective communication; practice healthy, responsible behaviors; and build functional, collaborative relationships. 

This I-Corps project is based on the development of a peripheral autonomic biofeedback training device as an effective process by which patients self-monitor heart rate, skin conductivity, peripheral skin temperature, and respiration rate while attempting to alter their internal responses. Breathing exercises and mindfulness techniques paired with biofeedback display has proven a powerful tool when teaching self-regulation of stress and anxiety. Not surprisingly, a number of studies have closely examined college student populations and their response to biofeedback training. The technology provides an emotion-aware, mental health and wellness platform that uses multimodal peripheral biofeedback, wireless sensor technology, and a goal-oriented software agent that will automatically refine the user experience based on the users’ real-time feedback from emotion-analyzing and gesture-tracking modules. Augmented by software agents, the interactive virtual objects will possess rich personality and emotional states flexible enough to respond to user’s interactions with intelligence and affective awareness. The results of this project will enable further development and translation of gamified, multimodal biofeedback training.

projectOutComesReport:
This project, Digital Therapeutics using autonomic regulation training for students challenged with debilitating stress, anxiety and depression, began with students taking PI Scott Ransom's Neural Engineering Tech Studio course in 2018.  The student team, called "Panic Away", developed a phone app and devised wearable electronics that would monitor a student's anxiety level and intervene with preprogrammed therapy before the onset of a panic attack.

Panic attacks are debilitating for students, causing missed classes, awkward social exchanges, and additional stress and anxiety about being in public.  Sufferers report an increasing desire to avoid people so that an attack does not happen in a social setting.

Therapies for such attacks are limited, and usually are not at the point-of-care.  The team's idea was to leverage the ubiquitous cell phone as a vehicle for therapy.

PanicAway’s initial prototype relies on a user with access to an iPhone and an Apple Watch that is acting as a heart-rate monitor. When a user’s heart rate exceeds a certain threshold, PanicAway goes to work, first prompting the user and then offering a number of coping features via the phone app.

Their work caught the interest of Geekwire, which published a story about the students and the course (see link below).

 UW students rely on input from professor’s son to create prototype for app that eases panic attacks - GeekWire

After completing the class, the team paired with LifeSpan Digital Health, which provided additional resources and leadership for the project.   

The iCorps grant allowed the team to explore several avenues and develop a minimally viable product (MVP).  During the course of the iCorps program the team was mentored by program faculty and provided funds for travel to do customer discovery.  Over the course of the program the team interivewed over 120 individuals including patients, therapists, counselors, and parents to build an understanding of product-market fit. 

One of the outcomes from this work was the importance of addressing under-served markets.  Minority and low income students indicated a large need for access to these types of therapies.  Access to other therapies is limited in these communities.  Providing this therapy to these groups became a priority for the team.

The customer discovery provided through this grant also helped the team narrow their student focus.  Originally the team was targeting students across academic years, but after conducting customer discovery interviews they realized the two greatest needs were with high school seniors and college freshman.  Students in these transitional years had the greatest incidence of anxiety and panic attacks.  The team decided to focus their efforts on counselors and support groups in these institutions.

The grant provided access to school counseling centers, which are currently partnering with the team to pilot their device and app to students in need, free of charge.  These first-use cases will validate several aspects of the therapy and aid the team in developing future iterations.

Due to the global pandemic, the grant monies earmarked for travel for customer discovery interviews and conference attendance could not be used.  That money was returned to NSF.  Although NSF was able to provide a no-cost extension, and travel restrictions have been lifted as of the time of this writing, the extension was unable to keep the grant active until travel was once again allowed.

While it is unfortunate that the team could only make use of a portion of the grant funds, they made the most with what they had.  They leveraged Zoom and other virtual meeting platforms to engage in customer discovery, and drove to local universities and high schools to meet with counselors and students when such visits were allowed.

Overall the customer discovery results and mentoring provided by the iCorps team were invaluable in helping the team develop their MVP and target appropriate markets, providing the initial product-market fit necessary to progress the therapy further.

abstractText:
In the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, American families are rapidly adapting to new conditions that disrupt how we work, perform childcare, and conduct education. Workforce, education, and social experiences are suddenly transformed, as millions of families are forced to take ownership of their children's education while working full-time or enduring hardships of new unemployment. Technology’s role is crucial, as this new social distancing context requires everything outside the family unit to now be performed remotely, over computer networks. This research project will develop understanding of the effects of these extraordinary circumstances on family life, educational outcomes, and work. The research team will investigate how digital technologies offer solutions, negatively impact, and perpetuate or reduce the digital divide and other disparities. To help families mitigate the negative effects of COVID-19 on society and the economy, the team will develop guidance—involving technologies in the home—about how to simultaneously support remote education, remote work, and family life. The research team will regularly communicate this guidance through blogging and social media targeted to families, educators, and technology designers.

This research will contribute empirical understanding of the experiences of families during COVID-19 social distancing and other times of disruption, in conjunction with computing and information by (1) collecting and analyzing data about how families’ social and educational experiences are transformed by social distancing in the COVID-19 pandemic; (2) investigating aspects of technology designs that are helpful and unhelpful to families and their relationships to social and economic institutions during COVID-19; (3) designing and discovering new technologies to support work-life balance, education, and family connectedness; and (4) deriving theories and models of how families in a pandemic crisis adapt technologies for distance learning and workforce participation. Thirty diverse families--each with at least one child between the ages of 3 and 13--will be remotely engaged in interviews, surveys, and design activities. The Asynchronous Remote Communities (ARC) method will be used to collect experiences and co-design new technologies. This method can benefit participants through increased reflection, social support, and resource-sharing. The team will develop new design artifacts based on remote co-design sessions with families. The work will contribute new methodologies, as the researchers adapt the ARC method for use with families with younger children in rapidly evolving situations. The research will be informed by, and potentially extend and further validate theoretical frameworks, including strength of weak ties, joint media engagement, family resilience theory, and funds of knowledge.

projectOutComesReport:
The COVID-19 pandemic upended the lives of families with young children as school closures and social distancing requirements left caregivers struggling to facilitate educational experiences, maintain social connections, and ensure financial stability. This research aimed to document parents' lived experiences adapting to technology's outsized role alongside other shifts associated with the pandemic and develop guidelines for technology's role in crisis situations.

This research brought together human-centered computing researchers working with children and families to achieve the following goals:

  1. Identify the top barriers and benefits of technologies used by families with kids aged 3-13 during COVID-19 in engaging in remote learning and socialization

  2. Experiment with participatory design methods that enable asynchronous, remote collaboration between families to design solutions that address needs within the pandemic context 

  3. Share outcomes with stakeholders invested in supporting families through understanding both their practical challenges and needs and their cultural resiliencies

To accomplish these goals, the team conducted an asynchronous remote communities study with 30 diverse US families with children aged 3 to 13 during the first several months of the COVID pandemic as lock-downs occurred and families struggled to learn and adapt. Over 10 weeks, the 30 families answered prompts on the Slack platform and participated in co-design activities on topics such as work-related needs, remote schooling, and caregiving mediated by technology. Prompts were intended to build on each other, with the first few weeks focusing on understanding participant needs, the next few weeks including refinement of parents' top concerns, and the final few weeks focusing on collaboratively envisioning design solutions. 

The study found that amidst gaps in infrastructural support from schools, workplaces, and communities, parents experienced deep anxiety and took on new roles, including tech support, school administrator, and curator of meaningful activities for their children. As parents shared bold and creative technology-based solutions for improving family well-being, schooling experiences, social life, and beyond, they demonstrated their capacity to contribute to new models of learning and family life. The study concluded that family-centered solutions are not only technology-oriented but must also account for intensive multi-tasking expected of parents, economic and social pressures, and screen-time overuse. Most parents outlined significant educational technology issues, including non-intuitive interfaces, poor troubleshooting guidance, and an inability for their children to use technology independently. The findings have implications for designers to attend to the balance between parent's values around technology use and desired vision for remote-based learning. Methodologically, this study found that the asynchronous, creative collaboration through playful and open-ended prompts lays the groundwork for cultivating family resilience.

Intellectual Merit: This research contributed an empirical understanding of the experiences families are facing during an unprecedented time and how technology played a role. The team co-designed new design artifacts based on remote co-design sessions with families. The work contributed new methods as the researchers adapted and critically reflected on the asychronus remote communities method for use with families with younger children and in rapidly evolving situations.

Broader Impacts: This research directly supported the 30 diverse families participating in co-design by helping support them in finding community and reflecting on their experiences. The team also communicated findings regularly through the project blog and social media. The team worked with an education non-profit and a foundation to translate findings for a more general design audience through reports and presentations. Finally, the research team held open office hours with the tech industry to directly translate the findings on how families could be better supported by technology design.

abstractText:
Situated on opposite sides of the Pacific Ocean, the US Pacific Northwest Region and Japan face significant earthquake risks from similar geophysical conditions. The Pacific Northwest is considered overdue for a Cascadia Subduction Zone 8.0–9.2 magnitude megaquake. When it happens, the estimated direct fatalities for Oregon and Washington states are up to 10,000, with economic losses of more than $80 billion. For the comparably sized region of Japan facing a Nankai megathrust earthquake, estimated fatalities are 80,000–323,000 lives and about $900 billion in economic loss. In the immediate aftermath of a megaquake, most of the disaster response agencies and personnel, if not all, will be overwhelmed and many neighborhoods in the region will need to rely on themselves to maintain essential activities for a prolonged period. To support these essential activities, communications will need to be robust enough to function under highly uncertain circumstances, and to enable real-time and reliable information sharing for efficient resource allocation and matching. This proposal represents the US portion of a planning grant for a collaboration with researchers from multiple Japanese Universities as part of the NSF/JST collaboration for the Smart and Connected Community Program.

This planning grant builds the capacity of a partnership of engineers and planners on both sides of the Pacific Ocean (Seattle area and Japan) to developing these critically needed communications and information-sharing technologies. The joint team will partner with three communities in Washington State and the city of Nagoya in Japan, to ensure that initial technical prototype ideas have real, place-specific relevance and applicability. Focus groups and community workshops will identify specific community needs, values, resources and concerns, and provide a feedback loop for evaluating the prototypes. It is expected that by working with these communities, the technological tools to be developed will be socially integrated, not only helping communities to address the critical need to prepare for a possible mega-earthquake but also to enhance resilience in the face of a wide range of life uncertainties and disruptions, and to improve communities’ daily quality of life.

projectOutComesReport:
Project overview. Situated on the two sides of the Pacific Ocean, the Seattle (Washington) and Nagoya (Japan) regions face significant earthquake risks from similar geophysical conditions. It is not a question of if it will happen, but when it will happen. When it happens, the estimated direct fatalities for Washington and Oregon are up to 10,000, with direct economic losses of more than $80 billion. By comparison, the similarly sized area of Japan affected by a Nankai megathrust earthquake would likely suffer 80,000-323,000 fatalities and economic losses of up to $900 billion. In the immediate aftermath of a megaquake, all disaster response agencies and personnel will be completely overwhelmed. For many, external help is unlikely to come immediately after a disaster. In anticipation, neighborhoods in both the Seattle and Nagoya regions are urged to prepare for community-based survival for up to 3 weeks, and this means that residents must be able to share information and respond in a timely manner to carry out essential activities (e.g., staying cool/warm in summer/winter, having food to eat, and having water) during this 3-week post-disaster period. The ultimate goal of a future SCC full grant is to develop effective socially-integrated technological solutions to enhance the ability of neighborhoods for real-time responses and survival. This planning grant explored three types of technologies:

●      technologies for supporting robust communications under highly uncertain environments;

●      technologies that enable real-time information gathering and sharing (while considering privacy);

●      technological solutions for efficient resource matching by leveraging social ties.

The planning project conducted community engagement of three communities (Laurelhurst, South Park and Westport) in Washington State and the city of Nagoya in Japan. The three communities in WA differ in their urban/rural and socio-economic status. More specifically, we carried out four probabilistically based random surveys in the four sites as well as focus groups and interviews with community members and stakeholders. Key results are reported below.

Willingness to share. We assess individuals’ willingness to share essential resources following a large disaster using data gathered from three communities in the Pacific Northwest of the U.S. and Nagoya, Japan, two regions that anticipate experiencing a magnitude 9.0 megaquake based on historical patterns of seismic activity. We find that willingness to share resources varied according to both resource type and the nature of the respondent’s social ties to the recipient. Having strong social ties with the recipient was slightly more important for Nagoya and South Park respondents than for Westport and Laurelhurst respondents, with Nagoya having the highest share of “strong ties only” responses for all resources except sanitation. We also find that levels of trust and strength of social ties strongly influence willingness to share in both countries. There are also patterns of difference in willingness to share specific resources across cultural contexts.

Community resource sharing for disaster preparedness. We explored (1) Resource Matching, (2) Information Sharing, and (3) Community Leadership and Civic Participation as dimensions of peer-to-peer sharing for more efficient distribution of local resources under “islanded” conditions in a regional disaster. Key findings are:

  • Resource matching: all community leaders made it clear: their agencies and organizations are not in a position to provide sufficient emergency resources to their communities in the event of an isolating disaster;
  • Information sharing: Many participants expressed a strong disapproval of the way certain platforms are actually used by their communities. The most commonly stated concerns were about community surveillance and the overwhelming negativity present on social media, especially Nextdoor.
  • Civic participation. While individual community members will likely turn to one another first in a disaster for information and resources, community leaders are a critical node in communication from the government to the community and vice versa. During our interviews, existing community leaders overwhelmingly described their role as one of curators of vital information.

Social media data extraction. We design a framework for text mining that will extract crisis

situation and location information from tweets about individuals in need. Using these extracted data, we develop a community source map of the disaster. There have been previous efforts to develop real-time disaster maps, but these are limited to manual entry whereas we use AI to create such maps. While much of the prior work focuses on densely populated urban scenarios, we also consider sparsely populated rural contexts where social network updates may be infrequent. We have experimented our proposed solution on around 20 different disaster related tweet databases from different part of the world. The primary results show ~81 percent accuracy in crisis situation information extraction and ~92 percent accuracy in location extraction.
