projectOutComesReport:
Efficient power generation scheduling approaches are crucial for current power system operations, in order to maintain system reliability while reducing carbon emissions. The objective of this project is to derive data-driven risk-averse stochastic optimization models and discover strong valid inequalities with efficient decomposition algorithms for the power generation scheduling problems with renewable energy integration, so as to ensure cost effectiveness and system robustness. We have successfully achieved this main objective with the following major outcomes:

1.     Optimal power flow (OPF) is an important tool for power system operators to deal with the power generation management. We successfully developed a data-driven risk-averse stochastic formulation to address the OPF problem considering the renewable generation uncertainty, to help power system operators transform historical information data into actionable insights and facilitate their decision-making process for the daily OPF scheduling. Our experiments show that the model can effectively balance the system robustness and cost effectiveness in addressing the OPF problem. In addition, we successfully extended the two-stage model into a multi-stage model so that we can utilize the revealed data information sequentially to further increase the system reliability and cost-efficiency.

2.     It is known that demand response (DR) can help reduce the peak-hour electricity consumption and accommodate the renewable generation output uncertainty. However, DR will inject another dimension of uncertainty to the system and it is hard to model. In this project, we successfully developed a data-driven multi-stage OPF model under both renewable generation and demand response uncertainties, with the objective of maximizing the total social welfare. We studied how the data of renewable generation and demand response pattern influent the decision-making process. We showed that our model led to a more reliable and cost-effective solution due to the effective utilization of data and the allowance of ambiguity of the distributions.

3.     We extended the case of considering the uncertainties of demand response and renewable energy output to a more general one: what if there are more distributed energy resources (DER) in the system? Currently, ISOs have limited control over the DERs connected to the grid, because most of these DERs are invisible to ISOs. We consider a recently developed concept, the Virtual Power Plant (VPP), which can aggregate small DERs and enable them to efficiently participate into the market to provide energy and ancillary services. We developed an innovative distributionally robust optimization model to help VPPs to optimally characterize the parameters in their bidding offers to the ISO for the reliability unit commitment run. We also successfully developed a tractable reformulation of the DR model, which can be implemented effectively by off-the-shelf solvers.

4.     To better comply with the day-ahead unit commitment schedules and hedge against the intermittent wind energy generation, we successfully developed an incentive-based coordination mechanism between a wind energy supplier and a conventional energy supplier by employing the concept of swing option contracts. The Pareto improvement can be achieved for wind and conventional energy suppliers.

 

The outcomes of this project can benefit both power system operators (such as Independent System Operators) for achieving cost efficiency and system reliability, and market participants (such as utilities) for maximizing their total profits. The outcomes of this project have been disseminated to other researchers and practitioners by 8 journal publications, 3 conference proceedings, 2 PhD dissertations, 1 master thesis, and more than 10 seminar and conference talks.

 

The results of research outcomes are incorporated into the course works: the graduate level course "Optimization under uncertainty" in Oklahoma State University and "Integer Programming" in University of Washington. This project has trained students to utilize advanced stochastic optimization under uncertainty and integer programming techniques to solve upfront power system problems with renewable energy integration, which accordingly contributes to the professional development of graduate students.

abstractText:
As the backbone of the U.S. energy infrastructure, the electric grid transmits power to the nation, with a revenue of around 400 billion dollars annually.  The electric grid is vulnerable to a variety of weather-related natural disasters.  The evaluation and mitigation of disruption-related risks and impacts are often computationally prohibitive due to the complexity of the power system, uncertainty of weather conditions, and the combinatorial nature of component failures.  This project will advance the use of analytical models and scalable solution methods to assist system operators to better evaluate and mitigate disruptions.  The PIs, as well as their graduate students, will collaborate with a U.S. Department of Energy national laboratory, which will facilitate connections with power systems operators.

This award will study a new class of data-driven optimization methodologies to support strategic and operational planning in power systems management.  As part of this research, the PIs will study probabilistic modeling of electricity grid disruptions based on meteorological and historical transmission availability data.  These data will be incorporated in distributionally robust optimization (DRO) models to (a) conduct risk assessment analysis, (b) harden pre-disaster electricity grid, (c) take corrective actions during disasters, and (d) conduct post-disaster self-healing and system restoration. The DRO approach will allow the consideration of an exponential number of disruptions, as well as their probabilities of occurring, to be inferred from the analysis of the data. In addition, this project will investigate new DRO solution approaches based on mixed-integer programming.

According to assessments by the National Research Council and the U.S. Global Change Research Program, U.S. energy infrastructure is increasingly vulnerable to severe weather due to the climate change. This project aims to address critical resilience challenges facing our nation’s power system infrastructure under natural disasters or unexpected disruptions. More specifically, we study probabilistic modeling of power grid contingency based on meteorological and historical transmission availability data. Then, we incorporate the data analytics in distributionally robust optimization models to (1) conduct risk assessment analysis, (2) harden pre-disaster power grid, (3) take corrective actions during disasters, and (4) conduct post-disaster self-healing and system restoration.

 

The research findings of this project include (1) Efficient utilization of available meteorological and transmission data to learn probabilistic models of the contingency probability distribution, (2) Reliable transmission line hardening planning framework to hedge against the risk of uncertain power flows and contingencies injected by the high penetration of renewable energy and extreme weather, (3) Effective distribution system topology plan to enhance the economic operation, resilience, and reliability of the power grid, and (4) Two reliability analysis models to quantify potential risks of having component outages for transmission system hardening plans. These research findings provide a clear picture of how we improve the resilience of power system infrastructure based on available historical data. This is particularly beneficial for maintaining the energy system reliability as natural disasters become more frequent and as renewable energy rises in the energy mix.

 

The outcomes of this project have been disseminated to other researchers and practitioners by eight journal papers, two conference proceedings, two PhD dissertations, one master thesis and multiple conference presentations. The results of research outcomes are incorporated into the course works: the graduate level course "Optimization under uncertainty" in Oklahoma State University and "Integer Programming" in University of Washington. This project has trained students to utilize advanced stochastic optimization under uncertainty and integer programming techniques to solve upfront power system problems, which accordingly contributes to the professional development of graduate students.

abstractText:
People often have difficulty in expressing their information needs. Many times this results from a lack of clarity regarding the task at hand, or the way an information or search system works. In addition, people may not know what they do not know. The former is addressed by search systems by providing recommendations, whereas there are no good solutions for the latter problem. Even when a search system makes recommendations, they are limited to suggesting objects such as queries and documents only. They do not consider providing suggestions for strategies, people, or processes. This project will address such problems by investigating the nature of the work a person is doing, predicting the potential problems they may encounter, and providing help to overcome those problems. Such a help could be an object such as a document or a query, a strategy, or a person. This whole process is referred to as Information Fostering. Beyond creating a general-purpose recommender system, Information Fostering is an idea for providing proactive suggestions and help to information seekers. This could allow them to avoid potential problems and capture promising opportunities in search before it is too late. In order to meet these goals, the project will carry out three lab studies. Through these studies, a new system will be created. This system will be integrated in a user's Web browser to provide real-time assessment of the information seeking process, as well as recommendations for queries, documents, strategies, and people. The outcomes of this project will make it possible and easier for a user with even low information literacy to be able to leverage the power of information. Such users may use information for multiple life contexts, including healthcare (e.g. caring for a sick family member), financial well-being (e.g., deciding on an investment portfolio), work (e.g., reviewing a business proposition), and education (e.g., compiling a report).

Current systems face challenges in understanding the problems that information seekers face due to their inability to express their information needs, recognizing a potential problem during a search episode, and identifying support needed that goes beyond what a typical search system could provide. Most recommender systems try to mitigate these problems by suggesting information objects (queries, documents), disregarding a deeper understanding of the task at hand or the possibility of recommendations that involve process/strategy, people, and other forms. The project will advance our understanding of these information-seeking problems at the task level, and of when and how help could be offered to information seekers. The offered help would go beyond recommending alternative queries and documents and would include recommending search strategies. This will be done in three phases with different user studies: (1) extracting the nature of task, problems, and help to build Task Model and Problem-Help Model; (2) testing the validity of Task Model and Problem-Help Model in being able to detect tasks, problems, and help; and (3) creating an Information Fostering system and evaluating its effectiveness in various search tasks. There will be three major intellectual outcomes: (1) Task Model that detects the nature of a search task using implicit signals such as browsing behaviors; (2) Problem-Help Model that uses behavioral data and other contextual factors, including the nature of the task, to explicate possible problems and potential solutions without explicitly asking from the searchers; and (3) a general-purpose recommender system framework, called Information Fostering, that proactively creates recommendations in real time for enhancing one's information seeking process and helping one avoid potential problems or grab an opportunity before it is too late. The results from this project will be disseminated through the project website, which will include technical reports, publications, and links to datasets and open-source software developed in this project.

People often have difficulty in expressing their information needs. Many times this results from a lack of clarity for the task at hand, or the way an information or search system works. In addition, people may not know what they do not know. The former is addressed by search systems by providing recommendations, whereas there are no good solutions for the latter problem. Even when a search system makes recommendations, they are limited to suggesting objects such as queries and documents only. They do not consider providing suggestions for strategies, people, or processes. This project addressed such problems by investigating the nature of the work a person is doing, predicting the potential problems they may encounter, and providing help to overcome those problems. This whole process is referred to as Information Fostering. Beyond creating a general-purpose recommender system, Information Fostering is an idea of providing proactive suggestions and help to information seekers. This could allow them avoid potential problems and capture promising opportunities in search before it is too late.

Through a carefully executed set of experiments and studies, the project resulted in the following outcomes.

  • Predictive model for proactive identification of query failure [empirical]
  • Predictive model for inferring potential problems and solutions [empirical]
  • Predictive model for identifying local states of complex search tasks [empirical]
  • A new version of Coagmento system that allows one to collect behavioral data from a user and act as a browser-based interface to provide recommendations [practical]
  • A conceptual model for the information seeking process [theoretical]
  • A systematic review of task dimensions and predictors [theoretical]
  • A demonstration of the framework to generate synthetic search sessions [practical]
  • A task representation model using Graph Neural Network [empirical]

Through these several strands of works, the project has shown how to understand, represent, and use task information from an information seeking session. The applications of this has been shown in various search and recommendation situations, demonstrating how such information can be useful and even critical in helping information seekers through proactive recommendations.

These outcomes are reported in several peer-reviewed papers at various conferences and journals. Many of them are also integrated in several PhD dissertations. Overall, about 20 papers/posters/demos at prestigious conferences or journals have resulted from this project. The project also helped produce five PhD dissertations. In addition, two postdocs and more than a dozen undergraduate and masters students were trained through this project. The two demos (Coagmento system and a synthetic data generation tool) are available as open-source distributions, which can help other researchers and developers.

abstractText:
Nonlinear evolution equations, also known as soliton equations, are used to model a wide variety of physical systems, such as ocean waves or fiber optic communications. Many such equations, for example the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation for waves in shallow water, have the exciting feature that many of their solutions can be given exactly by an explicit formula. This allows one to develop a precise understanding of the underlying physical processes. However, the range of conditions for which exact solutions are currently known is restrictive, inhibiting the use of such solutions in real-world applications. This project aims to find larger families of exact solutions to soliton equations, and use these solutions to develop statistical theories of the corresponding physical systems. 
  
The main goal of the project is to construct and study new families of solutions of soliton equations such as KdV, Nonlinear Schrödinger, and Kadomtsev-Petviashvili. These solutions are obtained as limits of multisoliton solutions, and are bounded and non-decreasing at infinity. They are described by a Riemann-Hilbert problem and can be efficiently computed numerically. The first goal is a rigorous mathematical description of these new solutions. The PIs will investigate to what extent these solutions solve the initial value problem for KdV and related systems. They will study spectral properties of the associated linear operators and construct non-periodic one-dimensional ideal conductors. Finally, the PIs will develop a statistical theory of integrable turbulence for KdV and other soliton equations.

projectOutComesReport:
The goal of our project has been to construct a new broad class of solutions to partial differential equations (PDEs) integrable by means of the inverse  scattering transform. But what is the significance of this problem from practical point of view? In modern times, many of us rely on the technology that allows fast communication all over the world. At the core of transatlantic communications are fiber optic lines that allow information transport between continents. The communication is achieved by sending trains of bits, that are represented by periodic electromagnetic pulses. However, a pulse that exits a fiber optic cable is not identical to the pulse that entered the fiber at the origin. The pulse may change it properties through effects of dispersion and nonlinear effects inherent to the fiber material. The evolution of a pulse in fiber is described by the nonlinear Schroedinger equation (NLSE), and it happens to be one of the PDEs integrable by the inverse scattering transform.

  The NLSE has been a subject of extensive studies, yet there are many open questions that still remain. We have constructed a family of solutions of NLSE, or potentials, that are bounded, non-periodic and yet not vanishing. An optical fiber of length of one thousand kilometers contains no less than 10 billion optical pulses, and thus may be considered as a bounded, non-vanishing and non-periodic potential, or a primitive potential. We developed a technique for finding primitive potentials by means of solving an auxiliary problem, that is related to NLSE by the so-called inverse scattering transform. We constructed these solutions numerically and generalized this approach to other integrable systems. The technique developed within the framework of this project has been generalized to solutions of KdV and KP equations for water waves. In addition we found clues that indicate of a possibility of integrating the 2D Euler equations with a free surface.

  Moreover, the results of present project lay the foundation for the study of turbulence in integrable systems, a new field of research that is relevant for many systems described by PDEs solvable by means of the inverse scattering transform. The present project contributed to support of graduate students, across several universities, publication of results in peer-reviewed journals and
dissemination of results at conferences. The overall goals of the proposed project have been completed successfully, and new directions of research have been found.
